title: Long-running job supervisors should safe-halt on failure spikes
summary: A supervisor that restarts every failed long-running job can turn a transient network, provider, or database outage into an infinite retry storm unless it detects rapid failure growth and stops for attention.
ai_value: When agents build keepalive loops, they should specify both the restart condition and the stop condition, including evidence that future operators can use to decide whether to resume.

contexts: imports, backfills, scrapers, sync jobs, report generation, and external API workers
jobs use tunnels, provider APIs, browser sessions, or remote databases that can fail independently of job logic
operator wants unattended progress but not uncontrolled mutation or retries

trigger_signals.description: Many failures share the same transport or connection class within a short window.
trigger_signals.pattern: ECONNREFUSED|connection closed|timeout|rate limit|5xx|failed count increased rapidly
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Prefer safe halt and handoff over blind restart.

trigger_signals.description: The supervisor has a restart loop but no failure threshold, backoff cap, or stop reason artifact.
trigger_signals.pattern: while true|restart always|nohup loop|no threshold|no halt condition
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add a stop condition before relying on unattended execution.

negative_signals.description: The job is read-only, externally idempotent, cheap, and already has exponential backoff plus alerting.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Automatic retries may be acceptable when blast radius and cost are bounded.

negative_signals.description: A human explicitly authorized an emergency retry loop with a time/cost bound and monitoring owner.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Some operational incidents require aggressive retries, but only with explicit bounds.

common_wrong_assumptions: A retry loop is safer than stopping because it needs less human attention.
Connection failures are harmless if the write path is idempotent.

first_checks.check: Define maximum consecutive failures, maximum failure rate, backoff behavior, and the artifact written when the supervisor stops.
first_checks.why: Future agents need to know whether the stop was intentional protection or a crash.

first_checks.check: After a safe halt, inspect the latest failure classes before resuming instead of only checking whether the process is dead.
first_checks.why: The process may have stopped because the guard worked as designed.

decision_rules.condition: Failures spike in a way consistent with transport/provider outage rather than isolated item-level errors.
decision_rules.then: Stop the loop, write counts and failure classes, and require a deliberate resume after diagnosis.

do_not: Do not implement Restart=always or while-true loops without a failure-spike stop condition for mutable long-running jobs.
Do not treat a guarded safe halt as an incident by itself; inspect the stop reason first.
Do not publish private service names, tunnel targets, account IDs, URLs, or organization-specific queue names in public lessons.

Do not confuse failure-spike safe halts with production-incident-safe-halt-scope-boundary; cross-check that record when the stop reason is an irreversible or approval boundary rather than retry-storm protection.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When creating or reviewing a supervisor, require both restart criteria and safe-halt criteria with a durable stop summary.

risk.notes: Candidate generalizes one private supervised import halt; thresholds and retry policy must be adapted to each system's cost and mutation risk.

sources.supports: A long-running job supervisor stopped after rapid connection failures and left a summary for morning attention, avoiding uncontrolled retries.
